Immersing part of the tube both **shortens** the air column and turns the **open** pipe
into a **closed** one.
**Step 1 — use the original frequency to fix v/L.** Open at both ends, of length L:
f = v/(2L) = 390 Hz
so **v/L = 780** ✓
**Step 2 — find the new air column.** With one quarter immersed, three quarters of the
tube still holds air:
air column = **3L/4** ✓
and the water surface forms a **closed** end.
**Step 3 — apply the closed-pipe formula.**
f′ = v/(4 x air column)
= v/(4 x 3L/4)
= **v/(3L)** ✓
**Step 4 — substitute.**
f′ = 780/3
= **260 Hz** ✓
**Why the pitch falls.** Two changes act in opposite directions ✓
shortening the column from L to 3L/4 would **raise** the pitch by 4/3
closing one end **halves** it
and the net factor is (4/3)/2 = **2/3**, giving 390 x 2/3 = **260 Hz** ✓ The closing
wins.
**Why a closed pipe sounds an octave lower.** A closed pipe fits only a **quarter**
wavelength in its length, an open pipe a **half** ✓ so for the same length the closed
pipe's wavelength is twice as long and its frequency half as great.
**A check with real numbers.** Taking v = 340 m s⁻¹:
L = v/2f = 340/780 = **0·436 m**
air column = 0·327 m, and a closed pipe of that length sounds
340/(4 x 0·327) = **260 Hz** ✓
**The general result.** For an open tube of fundamental f with a fraction x immersed,
f′ = **f/[2(1 − x)]** ✓
Here x = 1/4 gives 2f/3 = 260 Hz; and x = **1/2** would give exactly **f** - the two
effects cancelling, which is the companion question.
**Why the end correction is ignored.** A real open end resonates as though the tube were
about 0·6r longer ✓ For a narrow tube the correction is small, and these questions
neglect it.
**Reading the distractors.** **390 Hz** ✗ assumes nothing changes. **520 Hz** ✗ is
390 x 4/3, accounting for the shortening but keeping the pipe **open** - the commonest
error. **130 Hz** ✗ is 390/3, an over-correction ✓
∴ 260 Hz.

Newton's law of cooling makes the rate proportional to the **excess temperature**, so
compare rate against excess in each case.
**Step 1 — state the law.**
dT/dt = −k(T − T_s) ✓
with T_s = 30 °C.
**Step 2 — handle the first cooling.** From 90 °C to 89 °C:
drop ΔT = **1 °C**
mean temperature = **89·5 °C**, so the excess is **59·5 °C** ✓
1/t₁ = k(59·5), giving **t₁ = 1/(59·5k)** ✓
**Step 3 — handle the second.** From 60 °C to 59·5 °C:
drop ΔT = **0·5 °C**
mean temperature = **59·75 °C**, so the excess is **29·75 °C** ✓
0·5/t₂ = k(29·75), giving **t₂ = 0·5/(29·75k) = 1/(59·5k)** ✓
**Step 4 — compare.**
**t₂ = t₁** ✓
**Why they come out equal.** The second cooling is through **half** the temperature
drop, but at **half** the excess temperature - so the rate is halved too ✓ Halving both
the distance and the speed leaves the time unchanged. The question's numbers are chosen
precisely so the two factors cancel.
**The approximation used.** For a small drop, the rate may be evaluated at the **mean**
temperature of the interval ✓ Here the drops are 1 °C and 0·5 °C against excesses of
about 60 °C and 30 °C, so the approximation is excellent.
**Why Newton's law holds only for small excesses.** It is the linearisation of Stefan's
T⁴ law ✓ For T close to T_s,
T⁴ − T_s⁴ ≈ 4T_s³(T − T_s), which is linear. For large differences the true cooling is
much faster than Newton predicts.
**A worked instance.** With k = 0·01 per second:
t₁ = 1/(59·5 x 0·01) = **1·68 s**
t₂ = 0·5/(29·75 x 0·01) = **1·68 s** ✓ identical.
**The exponential solution.**
T − T_s = (T₀ − T_s)e^(−kt) ✓
from which the same result follows exactly, with logarithms - but the mean-temperature
method is far quicker for small drops.
**Where the law is used.** Estimating the time of death from body temperature, timing
the cooling of castings, and the standard school experiment with a calorimeter ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **t₂ = 2t₁** ✗ accounts for the halved rate but not the
halved drop. **t₂ = t₁/2** ✗ does the reverse, and **t₂ = 4t₁** ✗ doubles one error ✓
∴ t₂ = t₁.

Each photon carries momentum **h/λ**, and n of them are **absorbed**, so the body gains
**nh/λ**.
**Step 1 — write the momentum of one photon.**
p = **h/λ** ✓
from de Broglie's relation, or equally from p = E/c with E = hc/λ.
**Step 2 — multiply by the number.**
total momentum delivered = **nh/λ** ✓
**Step 3 — apply conservation of momentum.** The photons are **absorbed**, so all their
momentum is transferred:
momentum gained by the body = **nh/λ** ✓
**Why the body's mass does not appear.** **Momentum**, not velocity, is asked for ✓
The mass would be needed to find the **speed**:
v = nh/(mλ) ✓ which is the second option - a real quantity, answering a different
question. Reading what is asked is the whole of the difficulty.
**Why absorption and reflection differ.** An **absorbed** photon delivers p = h/λ ✓ A
**reflected** one reverses its momentum and delivers **2h/λ** - twice as much. This is
why a shiny solar sail outperforms a black one by a factor of two.
**A worked instance.** 10²⁰ photons of 500 nm light absorbed by a 1 g body:
p = 10²⁰ x (6·63 x 10⁻³⁴)/(5 x 10⁻⁷) = **1·33 x 10⁻⁷ kg m s⁻¹** ✓
v = 1·33 x 10⁻⁷/10⁻³ = **1·3 x 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹** - a tenth of a millimetre per second, even
from 10²⁰ photons. Light's momentum is minute.
**Radiation pressure.** The force is the momentum delivered per second ✓
P = I/c for absorption, **2I/c** for reflection
Sunlight gives about **4·6 µPa** at the Earth - tiny, but enough to drive a solar sail
and to perturb satellite orbits measurably.
**Where it is dramatic.** **Comet tails** always point away from the Sun, pushed by
radiation pressure and the solar wind ✓ and **optical tweezers** use focused laser
beams to hold and move single cells.
**The energy delivered, for contrast.** E = nhc/λ ✓ which heats the body, while the
momentum pushes it.
**Reading the distractors.** **nh/(mλ)** ✗ is the resulting **velocity**. **mnh/λ** ✗
has an extra mass and the wrong dimensions, and **h/(mλ)** ✗ is one photon's velocity
contribution ✓
∴ nh/λ.

Three conductors in series carry the **same heat flow**, and the temperature divides in
proportion to their **thermal resistances**.
**Step 1 — write each thermal resistance.** With identical length and area, R_th = L/(kA)
is proportional to **1/k**:
A: **1/K**
B: 1/(2K) = **0·5/K**
C: 1/(K/2) = **2/K** ✓
**Step 2 — find the total.**
R_total = (1 + 0·5 + 2)/K = **3·5/K** ✓
**Step 3 — find the drop across A.** The 100 °C divides in proportion to the
resistances:
ΔT_A = 100 x (1/K)/(3·5/K)
= 100/3·5
= **28·6 °C** ✓
**Step 4 — find the junction temperature.**
T = 100 − 28·6
= **71·4 ≈ 71 °C** ✓
**Why this is a potential divider.** Heat flow obeys the same mathematics as current ✓
temperature difference plays the part of voltage, heat flow that of current, and L/(kA)
that of resistance. Resistances in series divide the "voltage" in proportion.
**The full temperature profile.**
at the left end: **100 °C**
after A: **71·4 °C** ✓ a drop of 28·6
after B: 71·4 − 14·3 = **57·1 °C** - B's drop is half A's, since it conducts twice as
well
after C: 57·1 − 57·1 = **0 °C** ✓ C takes the largest drop, being the poorest conductor
**Why the poorest conductor dominates.** C, with half the conductivity of A, has
**twice** its thermal resistance and takes **four times** B's drop ✓ In any series
chain, the worst conductor controls the temperature profile - which is why a thin layer
of insulation is so effective.
**A check on the heat flow.** Taking K A/L = 1 in suitable units:
through A: 28·6/1 = **28·6**
through B: 14·3/0·5 = **28·6**
through C: 57·1/2 = **28·6** ✓ equal everywhere, as the steady state demands.
**What "steady state" means.** The temperatures have stopped changing, so no heat
accumulates anywhere ✓ Before that the specific heats matter and the problem becomes a
differential equation.
**Reading the distractors.** **29 °C** ✗ is the **drop** across A rather than the
junction temperature - the commonest slip. **63 °C** ✗ and **37 °C** ✗ correspond to
different conductivity orderings ✓
∴ 71.

Find the voltage across the parallel section from the heat in the 5 Ω, then work out
the heat in the series 2 Ω.
**Step 1 — identify the circuit.** The 6 Ω and 9 Ω are in **series**, giving **15 Ω**,
and that combination is in **parallel** with the 5 Ω ✓ The 2 Ω is in **series** with the
whole parallel block.
**Step 2 — use the given heat to find V²t.** For the 5 Ω,
H = V²t/R
4·05 = V²t/5
**V²t = 20·25** ✓
where V is the voltage across the parallel section.
**Step 3 — find the parallel resistance.**
R_p = (15 x 5)/(15 + 5)
= 75/20
= **3·75 Ω** ✓
**Step 4 — find the heat in the 2 Ω.** The same current I = V/R_p passes through it:
H₂ = I²R₂t
= (V/3·75)²(2)t
= 2V²t/14·0625 ✓
**Step 5 — substitute.**
H₂ = 2(20·25)/14·0625
= 40·5/14·0625
= **2·88 J** ✓
**A check on the whole circuit.** Taking t = 1 s, V² = 20·25 so **V = 4·5 V**:
current through 5 Ω: 4·5/5 = **0·9 A**, heat = 0·81 x 5 = **4·05 J** ✓
current through 15 Ω: 4·5/15 = **0·3 A**, heat = 0·09 x 15 = **1·35 J**
total current: **1·2 A**, heat in the 2 Ω = 1·44 x 2 = **2·88 J** ✓ exactly as found.
**Why the series resistor is treated by I²R.** The **current** is common to it and the
rest of the circuit ✓ For the parallel branches the **voltage** is common, so V²/R is
the natural form. Choosing the right form for each is the whole technique.
**How the current divides.** 0·9 A through the 5 Ω and 0·3 A through the 15 Ω, in the
**inverse** ratio of the resistances ✓ 3 : 1, as 15 : 5 demands.
**Where the power goes.** Total 4·05 + 1·35 + 2·88 = **8·28 J** ✓ and the supply
delivers (1·2)(4·5 + 2·4) = 8·28 J ✓ consistent.
**Reading the distractors.** **1·44** ✗ is I²t without the factor R = 2. **5·76** ✗ is
twice the answer, and **2·02** ✗ matches no step ✓
∴ 2.88.

Heat flows **along** the axis through both materials at once, so the two conductors are
in **parallel** and their conductivities add in proportion to **area**.
**Step 1 — see the geometry.** The ends are held at different temperatures and no heat
crosses the cylindrical surface, so heat flows **axially** through the core **and**
through the shell **side by side** ✓ That is a parallel arrangement.
**Step 2 — find the two areas.**
core, radius R: **πR²** ✓
shell, between R and 2R: π(2R)² − πR² = **3πR²** ✓
total: **4πR²**
**Step 3 — add the heat flows.** Both have the same length and the same temperature
difference:
(dQ/dt)_total = (K₁πR² + K₂ x 3πR²)ΔT/L ✓
**Step 4 — define the effective conductivity.** Writing this as K_eff(4πR²)ΔT/L:
K_eff(4πR²) = K₁πR² + 3K₂πR²
**K_eff = (K₁ + 3K₂)/4** ✓
**Why the shell has three times the core's area.** Area goes as r², and 4 − 1 = **3** ✓
Doubling the outer radius quadruples the total area, so the annulus between R and 2R is
three times the core.
**Why this is an area-weighted average.** In parallel, conductances add ✓ and each
conductance is proportional to its own area - so the effective conductivity is the mean
of K₁ and K₂ weighted by **1 : 3**.
**The electrical analogy.** Two resistors in parallel: conductances add ✓ Here the
"conductances" are K₁A₁/L and K₂A₂/L, and their sum defines K_eff A_total/L.
**The contrast with the series case.** Had the two materials been placed **end to end**
along the flow, the **resistances** would add and
K_eff = 2K₁K₂/(K₁ + K₂) ✓ the harmonic mean, which is the second distractor.
Recognising parallel from series is the crux of such questions.
**A check on the limits.**
K₂ = K₁: K_eff = 4K₁/4 = **K₁** ✓ a uniform cylinder, as it must be
K₂ = 0, a perfectly insulating shell: K_eff = **K₁/4** ✓ only the core conducts, over a
quarter of the total area.
**Why "no loss across the cylindrical surface" matters.** It guarantees the flow is
purely **axial** ✓ so the two materials act independently and the parallel treatment is
exact.
**Reading the distractors.** **K₁ + K₂** ✗ ignores the areas. **(3K₁ + K₂)/4** ✗
reverses the weighting, giving the core three times the shell's area ✓
∴ (K₁ + 3K₂)/4.
